query: Which method can be used for the presence of ferromagnetic ground states, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Spin‐polarized density functional theory (DFT) can be used to predict and identify ferromagnetic ground states in multi‐component (e.g., high‐entropy) alloys because it explicitly accounts for electron spin and exchange interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) or multi-component alloy suspected of having magnetic elements in a disordered solid solution state at its ground state composition.
generation.intervention: Apply spin‐polarized DFT calculations to determine the total energies for various spin configurations.
generation.conditions: Calculations at T ≃ 0 K using periodic boundary conditions and an appropriate exchange-correlation functional that properly captures electron correlation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The electron density distribution and the exchange splitting between spin-up and spin-down states.
generation.mechanism: In spin-polarized DFT, the inclusion of spin degrees of freedom enables the capture of exchange interactions that lower the total energy when spins align—this energy lowering indicates a ferromagnetic ground state if it is the most stable configuration.
generation.predicted_outcome: The spin-polarized DFT results will show that the lowest-energy state has finite magnetic moments aligned in the same direction (ferromagnetic ordering) relative to non-spin-polarized or antiferromagnetic configurations.
generation.baseline: Non-spin-polarized DFT calculations, which neglect the explicit treatment of the spin degree of freedom.
generation.boundary: The prediction may be sensitive to the choice of exchange-correlation functional and may not capture finite-temperature effects; thus the method is most reliable for ground state (T = 0 K) predictions.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is well established, quantitative predictions (e.g., the exact magnetic moment values and energy differences) can vary with computational parameters and approximations, leaving uncertainty in precise values.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform both spin-polarized and non-spin-polarized DFT calculations on a chosen HEA sample expected to exhibit ferromagnetism. Compare the computed ground state energy and magnetic moment with experimental magnetization data (e.g., measured via SQUID magnetometry) at low temperatures.
measurements: Total energy differences between spin configurations
Experimental hysteresis loops and magnetization curves from SQUID measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the spin-polarized DFT fails to predict a lower-energy ferromagnetic state (or predicts significantly different magnetic moments) compared with experimental results, then the hypothesis that spin-polarized DFT reliably predicts ferromagnetic ground states in the material is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].
